newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bourse in Bosnia? Not any time soon - expert.
newsitem.headline: Bourse in Bosnia? Not any time soon - expert.

text.p: Bosnia is unlikely to have a stock market any time soon because the country lacks capital and has little experience with share purchases, an independent economist said on Monday.

"I don't see a stock market in Bosnia soon for a number of reasons, the main one being that people would not be eager to buy shares even when the legal conditions for companies' share sales are fulfilled," economist Fikret Causevic told Reuters.
A year after Bosnia's 43-month war ended, the country is struggling hard to build a market economy with money from international donors.
The half of Bosnia run by a Moslem-Croat federation prepared a draft privatization law in June which has yet to be adopted by the federation parliament.
The draft would help to address the country's lack of capital by giving citizens vouchers to use to purchase company shares, flats and office space.

The voucher system was devised as a way for the cash- strapped Bosnian government to settle claims from its citizens for frozen bank accounts, soldiers' unpaid salaries and nationalized real property.
One Sarajevo newspaper estimated recently that the government owed 14 billion German marks in such claims.
Causevic said he expected Bosnians to respond cautiously to share purchase possibilities even with privatisation vouchers.
"People would prefer to have something concrete, like flats, rather than company shares even if someone persuaded them that a company would be successful enough to pay them back," he said.
Causevic said Bosnia has enough licensed banks to establish an over-the-counter inter-bank share market, which he felt would be an adequate substitute for a stock market for the time being.
"A stock market requires rigorous rules. If Bosnia set rules flexibly we could have companies that do not deserve to be on the market offering shares," he warned.
"On the other hand, if the rules were set properly we probably would have a few companies dominating the market and perhaps boosting their share prices unrealistically."
Causevic said 43 banks registered on Moslem-Croat federation and Serb republic territory in Bosnia would be sufficient to provide for a successful inter-bank market.
The legal requirements for such a market have been partially met with a 1994 law on money and capital markets.
But a state securities commission to supervise the issue of shares and bonds has yet to be created, Causevic said.
